'''Frederick C. Neidhardt''' (1931-2016) was an American [[microbiologist]] who was on the faculty at [[Purdue University]] and the [[University of Michigan]]. He is known for his work on the [[physiology]] and [[biochemistry]] of [[bacteria]]l growth and for early work in bacterial [[proteomic]]s.<ref name="stc">{{cite web|last1=Schaechter|first1=Elio|last2=Ingraham|first2=John|title=Frederick C. Neidhardt (1931 − 2016): An Obituary|url=http://schaechter.asmblog.org/schaechter/2016/10/frederick-c-neidhardt-19312016an-obituary.html|website=Small Things Considered|accessdate=12 January 2017}}</ref><ref name="umich">{{cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Memoir|url=http://faculty-history.dc.umich.edu/faculty/frederick-c-neidhardt/memoir|archive-url=|archive-date=|accessdate=June 4, 2020|website=University of Michigan Faculty History Project}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Neidhardt was born in [[Philadelphia]] on May 12, 1931.<ref name="aan">{{cite web|title=Frederick C. Neidhardt|url=http://obits.mlive.com/obituaries/annarbor/obituary.aspx?pid=182009824|website=Ann Arbor News|accessdate=12 January 2017|date=20 October 2016}}</ref> He was an undergraduate at [[Kenyon College]] and graduated in 1952. He then received his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1956.<ref name=stc /><ref name=umich /> He spent the next several years as a researcher at the [[Pasteur Institute]], the [[University Institute of Microbiology]], and the [[University of Regensburg]] before returning to the United States in 1961 for a faculty position at [[Purdue University]].<ref name=umich />

==Academic career==
Neidhardt's independent research career began when he joined the Purdue faculty in 1961. He remained there until 1970, when he moved to the [[University of Michigan]] to become the chair of the microbiology department; he continued as chair for the following 13 years.<ref name=umich /> During that time he served in a number of other administrative roles, including associate dean for faculty in the medical school and Vice President for Research.<ref name=aan /><ref name=umich /><ref name="umich_profile">{{cite web|title=Frederick C. Neidhardt, Ph.D.|url=F. G. Novy Distinguished University Professor|website=University of Michigan|accessdate=12 January 2017}}</ref> He became the [[Frederick G. Novy]] Distinguished University Professor of Microbiology and Immunology in 1989 and retired, assuming [[professor emeritus]] status, in 1999.<ref name=umich />

Neidhardt authored or coauthored several widely recognized textbooks and reference works, including an important treatise on bacterial growth titled ''Escherichia coli and Salmonella: Cellular and Molecular Biology''.<ref name=umich /> He spent almost twenty years on the board of the Waksman Foundation for Microbiology housed at [[Swarthmore College]] and served as its president.<ref name="swarthmore">{{cite web|title=Waksman Foundation for Microbiology Mourns the Passing of Former President Frederick C. Neidhardt|url=http://www.newswise.com/articles/waksman-foundation-for-microbiology-mourns-the-passing-of-former-president-frederick-c-neidhardt|website=Swarthmore College|accessdate=12 January 2017}}</ref> He served as the president of the [[American Society for Microbiology]] in 1982.<ref name=umich /><ref name=asm_milestone>{{Cite web|url=http://www.asm.org/index.php/71-membership/archives/93804-university-of-michigan-department-of-microbiology-and-immunology-designated-as-a-milestones-in-microbiology-site|title=University of Michigan Department of Microbiology and Immunology Designated as a Milestones in Microbiology site|last=|first=|date=|website=American Society for Microbiology|publisher=|access-date=13 January 2017|archive-date=16 January 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116144813/http://www.asm.org/index.php/71-membership/archives/93804-university-of-michigan-department-of-microbiology-and-immunology-designated-as-a-milestones-in-microbiology-site|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==

* [[Eli Lilly and Company-Elanco Research Award|Eli Lilly Award in bacteriology or immunology]], 1966<ref name=umich /><ref name=asm_milestone />
* [[Alice C. Evans Award]], 1983
* Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], 1996<ref name=umich /><ref name=aaas>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/content/system/search.aspx?s=frederick+neidhardt|title=Frederick C. Neidhardt|last=|first=|date=|website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|publisher=|access-date=13 January 2017}}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Neidhardt was a [[Quaker]] and was noted by friends for his dedication to social causes, including support for women and minority scientists.<ref name=stc /> Neidhardt had three children. He died on October 7, 2016, in [[Tucson, Arizona]], of injuries stemming from a fall.<ref name=aan />
